nodes.label: Magan — the copper of the Oman peninsula
nodes.full: Magan, the copper-producing land of the Oman peninsula, is the source of the metal that forms the backbone of Dilmun's transit trade — a distinct region (with its own folio) whose ore Dilmun brokers north to Mesopotamia by the tonne.
nodes.src: background — see the magan-3000bc-300bc folio

nodes.label: Meluhha — the Harappan Indus world
nodes.full: Meluhha, the Mesopotamian name for the Indus/Harappan civilisation, is the far end of the Gulf trade: the source of carnelian, ivory, timber and gold, and of the weight standard and seal types that meet the Mesopotamian ones at Dilmun.
nodes.src: background; Possehl, "The Indus Civilization" (2002)

nodes.label: Dilmun enters the cuneiform record
nodes.full: Dilmun appears in the earliest administrative tablets of Uruk and in the inscriptions of Ur-Nanshe of Lagash, who records ships of Dilmun bringing timber. From its first documentation Dilmun is defined by what it ships north, not by its kings.
nodes.src: Archaic Uruk texts; Ur-Nanshe of Lagash inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 1)

nodes.label: Sargon of Akkad — 'ships of Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha'
nodes.full: Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha moored at the quay of his capital. The formula fixes Dilmun as the nearest of the three Gulf trading lands and the gateway to the others.
nodes.src: Sargon of Akkad inscription (Frayne, RIME 2.1.1)

nodes.label: The walled capital at Qal'at al-Bahrain
nodes.full: Dilmun's peak: a fortified town of some 15 hectares at Qal'at al-Bahrain with a city wall, planned streets, warehouses and a temple, running the transit trade between Mesopotamia and the lands to the east. This is the Dilmun of the Ur merchant archives.
nodes.src: Højlund & Andersen, "Qala'at al-Bahrain" vol.1 (1994)

nodes.label: Uballissu-Marduk — Kassite governor of Dilmun
nodes.full: A cache of clay tablets from Qal'at al-Bahrain names Uballissu-Marduk, governor of Dilmun under the Kassite kings of Babylon, writing to subordinates about dates, taxes and personnel. Dilmun has become a Babylonian province run by an appointed official.
nodes.src: Nashef, the Bahrain Kassite governor letters

nodes.label: The Dilmun weight standard
nodes.full: Dilmun regulated Gulf trade with a standardised weight of about 13.4 grams and its multiples. Balance weights on this standard turn up from southern Mesopotamia to the Indus port of Lothal — a shared commercial measure Dilmun helped enforce.
nodes.src: Weisgerber; Roaf & Galbraith on Gulf weights

nodes.label: The Dilmun stamp seal as a legal instrument
nodes.full: Round stamp seals in a distinctive local style were used to seal jars, doors and clay tags, authenticating transactions. Their sudden appearance in quantity marks the moment Dilmun's trade became bureaucratised.
nodes.src: Kjærum, "The Stamp and Cylinder Seals" (1983)

nodes.label: The Kassite governor's archive
nodes.full: The Kassite-period tablets from Qal'at al-Bahrain record ration lists, date-palm accounting and the movement of workers — the paperwork of a provincial administration reporting to Babylon. Dilmun is now governed, not merely traded with.
nodes.src: Nashef; Højlund & Andersen vol.2 (1997)

nodes.label: Temple estates and offerings at Barbar
nodes.full: The Barbar temple complex controlled land, livestock and a sacred spring, receiving offerings recorded on sealed tags. In Dilmun as in Mesopotamia, the temple was an economic institution as much as a religious one.
nodes.src: Andersen & Højlund, "The Barbar Temples" (2003)

nodes.label: Failaka as Dilmun's northern administrative outpost
nodes.full: Failaka, at the head of the Gulf, held a fortified settlement with its own temple and hundreds of seals — an extension of the Dilmun administrative system placed to watch the approaches from Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Højlund, "The Bronze Age Pottery" (Failaka vol.2, 1987)

nodes.label: Inzak and Meskilak — the gods of Dilmun
nodes.full: Dilmun's chief god was Inzak, 'lord of Agarum', paired with the goddess Meskilak. Their names recur on seals and dedications from Bahrain to Failaka, and Mesopotamian god-lists slot Inzak in beside their own deities.
nodes.src: Nashef, "The Deities of Dilmun" (1986)

nodes.label: The Barbar water temple
nodes.full: Three temples were built one above another at Barbar around a stepped stone basin fed by a spring — a shrine to the sweet water that made Bahrain habitable. A copper bull's head and votive figures were found in its precinct.
nodes.src: Andersen & Højlund, "The Barbar Temples" (2003)

nodes.label: Serpent burials and ritual deposits
nodes.full: Bowls containing the bones of sea snakes, sometimes with a bead, were buried in the foundations of buildings at Qal'at al-Bahrain and in the Failaka temple. The practice links Dilmun ritual to the sea and the underworld.
nodes.src: Bibby, "Looking for Dilmun" (1969); Lombard

nodes.label: Dilmun as the pure land in Sumerian myth
nodes.full: In 'Enki and Ninhursag', Dilmun is a land 'pure, clean and bright' where no illness or death exists. Elsewhere the flood survivor Ziusudra is settled in Dilmun 'where the sun rises'. Mesopotamia imagined Dilmun as a paradise at the edge of the world.
nodes.src: 'Enki and Ninhursag' (ETCSL 1.1.1); the Sumerian Flood Story

nodes.label: The burial-mound landscape as an afterlife geography
nodes.full: Tens of thousands of low earth-and-stone mounds cover central Bahrain, each over a single chambered grave with a few pots, a seal and personal ornaments. The scale of the cemetery suggests a society that invested heavily in provisioning its dead.
nodes.src: S.F. Andersen, Bahrain Burial Mounds project; UNESCO (2019)

nodes.label: The Dilmun stamp-seal style
nodes.full: Dilmun seals are round, high-backed and cut with gazelles, seated figures drinking through straws, bull-men and stars — a coherent local iconography distinct from Mesopotamian and Indus glyptic. They are Dilmun's signature art form.
nodes.src: Kjærum (1983); Al-Sindi, "Dilmun Seals" (1999)

nodes.label: The Royal Mounds of A'ali
nodes.full: A cluster of two-storey stone-chambered tumuli up to 15 metres high and 45 across stands apart from the ordinary mound-fields. These are Dilmun's monumental tombs — the clearest sign of an emerging ruling class.
nodes.src: Danish expedition; UNESCO "Dilmun Burial Mounds" (2019)

nodes.label: The copper bull's head of Barbar
nodes.full: A hollow-cast copper head of a bull, once mounted on a lyre in the Mesopotamian manner, was found in the Barbar precinct. It is the finest surviving Dilmun metalwork and shows craftsmen working to a high Near Eastern standard.
nodes.src: Andersen & Højlund (2003); compare the bull-lyres of Ur

nodes.label: Barbar red ridged ware
nodes.full: Dilmun's characteristic pottery — thin, ring-based jars with a red slip and a rilled or ridged shoulder — was made in quantity on Bahrain and exported around the Gulf, a recognisable Dilmun brand in the archaeological record.
nodes.src: Højlund, "The Bronze Age Pottery" (Failaka vol.2, 1987)

nodes.label: The straw-drinking banquet on Dilmun seals
nodes.full: A recurring seal scene shows two seated figures drinking from a large jar through long straws, sometimes flanking a standard or an animal. The motif depicts a ritual feast, the nearest thing to a performance record Dilmun has left.
nodes.src: Kjærum (1983), the 'drinking scene' class

nodes.label: Scribes and cuneiform literacy at Qal'at al-Bahrain
nodes.full: The Kassite-period tablets prove trained scribes were working on Bahrain, writing Akkadian in the Babylonian manner. Dilmun was inside the cuneiform world, not merely visited by it.
nodes.src: Bahrain Kassite tablet archive (Nashef)

nodes.label: Weight-based reckoning across three trade systems
nodes.full: Dilmun merchants worked fluently between the Mesopotamian shekel, their own ~13.4 g standard and Indus binary weights, converting values across all three. This applied arithmetic of exchange was Dilmun's core professional knowledge.
nodes.src: Roaf; De Jesus on Gulf weight assemblages

nodes.label: 'Where the sun rises' — Dilmun in Mesopotamian cosmography
nodes.full: Mesopotamian texts place Dilmun at the sunrise edge of the inhabited world, the last land before the cosmic sea. It was a real place doing real trade, but it also marked the boundary of the Mesopotamian mental map.
nodes.src: Horowitz, "Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography" (1998)

nodes.label: Dilmun the entrepôt
nodes.full: Mesopotamian barley, wool, textiles, sesame oil and silver came south to Dilmun and were exchanged for copper from Magan and carnelian, ivory, timber and gold from Meluhha. Dilmun produced little of this itself; it took a cut on all of it.
nodes.src: Ur III and Old Babylonian 'Dilmun trade' texts; Leemans (1960)

nodes.label: The alik Tilmun merchants of Ur and Ea-nasir
nodes.full: At Ur, associations of 'those who go to Dilmun' financed copper voyages, pooling temple silver and private capital. One of them, Ea-nasir, is immortalised in a customer's clay tablet complaining that the copper he delivered was sub-standard and his manner rude.
nodes.src: The Ea-nasir archive from Ur (UET V 81); Oppenheim, JAOS 74 (1954)

nodes.label: Magan copper re-exported through Dilmun
nodes.full: Copper was the trade's backbone. Oman's ore reached Mesopotamia via Dilmun by the tonne — one Ur text logs over 18 tonnes in a single consignment — until Old Babylonian buyers began dealing with Magan directly.
nodes.src: Ur III copper-import texts (Leemans 1960); Weisgerber on Omani copper

nodes.label: The date gardens of Bahrain
nodes.full: Artesian springs let Bahrain grow dense date palm groves and cereals under them — the agricultural base that fed the towns and supplied dates as a trade good. Kassite accounts tax this palm cultivation directly.
nodes.src: Kassite governor tablets on date accounting (Nashef)

nodes.label: The entrepôt collapses, c.1700 BC
nodes.full: When Indus trade withered and Old Babylonian merchants bypassed Bahrain for direct Magan dealings, Dilmun's transit economy fell away. Qal'at al-Bahrain shrank; the great mound-building slowed. Dilmun continued, smaller, as a Kassite dependency.
nodes.src: Højlund on the City II-III transition; Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: Artesian well engineering
nodes.full: Dilmun builders sank stone-lined shafts to tap the artesian aquifer, most spectacularly the stepped water basin under the Barbar temple. Control of sweet water — including famous springs bubbling up offshore — underpinned everything else.
nodes.src: Barbar temple water installation (Andersen & Højlund 2003)

nodes.label: Chambered burial-mound construction
nodes.full: The larger Dilmun tombs use dressed stone chambers with corbelled or capstone roofs, ringwalls and, in the A'ali 'royal' mounds, two storeys — a repeatable engineering solution scaled up for elite burials.
nodes.src: Danish and Bahraini excavation of the A'ali mounds

nodes.label: Seagoing plank boats and the magilum-boat
nodes.full: Mesopotamian texts distinguish the large 'Magan-boat' and 'Dilmun-boat' from river craft. Reed hulls gave way to bitumen-sealed sewn-plank vessels able to carry tonnes of copper across open water in the summer sailing season.
nodes.src: Ship terminology in the Ur III texts (Potts 1995); Carter (2006)

nodes.label: The city wall of Qal'at al-Bahrain
nodes.full: City II was enclosed by a substantial stone-founded wall with towers and gates — the first monumental fortification in the Gulf, protecting the warehouses on which the whole trade depended.
nodes.src: Højlund & Andersen, "Qala'at al-Bahrain" vol.1 (1994)

nodes.label: Copper working on Bahrain
nodes.full: Crucibles, moulds and slag show Dilmun smiths casting tools, weapons and fine objects like the Barbar bull from imported copper, adding tin for bronze. Dilmun did not mine metal but it finished it.
nodes.src: Killick & Moon, "The Early Dilmun Settlement at Saar" (2005)

nodes.label: The Dilmun-Magan-Meluhha triangle
nodes.full: Akkadian royal inscriptions name Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha together as the three lands reached by sea. Dilmun was the hinge: goods from the Indus (Meluhha) and Oman (Magan) passed through Bahrain on their way to Mesopotamia and back.
nodes.src: Sargon of Akkad and Gudea of Lagash inscriptions; Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: Indus goods and weights at Dilmun
nodes.full: Etched carnelian beads, ivory, Indus-standard cubical weights and a handful of Indus-inscribed seals at Bahrain and Failaka show direct contact with Harappan ports. Dilmun sat where the Indus and Mesopotamian worlds physically met.
nodes.src: Indus weights and etched carnelian from Qal'at al-Bahrain and Failaka (Kjærum 1983)

nodes.label: The 'Gulf seal' as a shared trade script
nodes.full: Before the fully local Dilmun style crystallised, a round 'Persian Gulf' seal type — Mesopotamian technique, mixed motifs — circulated among Gulf and Indus merchants. One turned up at the Harappan port of Lothal, marking the network's far end.
nodes.src: Kjærum, "Seals of a Persian Gulf type"; the Lothal seal (S.R. Rao)

nodes.label: Tarut and the eastern Arabian mainland in the Dilmun world
nodes.full: Tarut island off Qatif produced Early Dynastic-style statuary, chlorite vessels and rich graves — a mainland partner (perhaps the original core) of the Dilmun polity before Bahrain became dominant. The 'land of Dilmun' straddled the water.
nodes.src: Masry, "Prehistory in Northeastern Arabia" (1974); Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: The Akkadian Empire names the Gulf lands
nodes.full: Sargon and his successors, projecting power to the sea, fixed 'Dilmun', 'Magan' and 'Meluhha' in the written record for the first time. The Gulf entered history as the maritime frontier of the world's first empire.
nodes.src: Old Akkadian royal inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2)

nodes.label: The decline of the Indus Civilisation
nodes.full: As Harappan cities were abandoned and the integrated Indus system unravelled, the Meluhha trade that fed Dilmun's entrepôt dried up. The event that ended one civilisation hollowed out the economy of another a thousand miles away.
nodes.src: Possehl, "The Indus Civilization" (2002); Potts (1990)

nodes.label: Kassite Babylon absorbs Dilmun
nodes.full: Under the Kassite dynasty, Babylon extended formal control over Dilmun, installing a governor and provisioning the island from the mainland. Dilmun spent the later Bronze Age as the seaward province of a Mesopotamian kingdom.
nodes.src: Kassite governor archive at Qal'at al-Bahrain; Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: The mounds are everyone's graves
nodes.full: Long read as the tombs of a privileged class, the Dilmun mounds are now understood as the cemetery of the whole population: men, women, infants, each in a single-chamber grave with a pot and a personal item. Monumental burial was a norm, not a privilege.
nodes.src: S.F. Andersen, Bahrain Burial Mounds project; UNESCO (2019)

nodes.label: Women buried with seals and ornament
nodes.full: A number of women's graves contain stamp seals — the instruments of commercial and legal life — alongside beads of gold, carnelian and shell. It suggests women in Dilmun could hold property and transact in their own right.
nodes.src: Saar cemetery (Killick & Moon 2005); Al-Sindi on the A'ali mounds

nodes.label: Infant jar-burials under the house floor at Saar
nodes.full: At the Saar village, dead infants were placed in pottery jars and buried beneath the floors of houses rather than in the mound cemetery — keeping the youngest dead within the household. Different rites marked different stages of belonging.
nodes.src: Killick & Moon, "The Early Dilmun Settlement at Saar" (2005)

nodes.label: A date-heavy diet written in Dilmun teeth
nodes.full: Skeletons from the mounds show heavy tooth wear and high rates of caries — the signature of a diet built on dates and other sugars, supplemented by fish. The trade wealth of Dilmun did not translate into robust health for most of its people.
nodes.src: Littleton & Frohlich, AJPA 101 (1996)

nodes.label: Naram-Sin's fleet and the Gulf as a war theatre
nodes.full: Naram-Sin of Akkad campaigned by sea against Magan and claims to have crossed 'the Lower Sea' with ships. Dilmun, the hinge of that sea, first appears in the record inside a world in which the dominant Mesopotamian power now projected armed force down the Gulf.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2.1.4); Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: The fortification of the entrepôt
nodes.full: City II was given a stone-founded wall with towers and gates — the first monumental fortification in the Gulf. The warehouses on which the whole transit trade depended now needed defending against raiding and piracy.
nodes.src: Højlund & Andersen, 'Qala'at al-Bahrain' vol.1 (1994)

nodes.label: The Sealand kings and the head of the Gulf
nodes.full: After the fall of Hammurabi's dynasty the First Sealand Dynasty held the marshland approaches to the Gulf, controlling and disrupting the sea route between Babylonia and Dilmun. One Sealand king bears a name compounded with the Dilmun god Inzak.
nodes.src: Dalley, 'Babylonian Tablets from the First Sealand Dynasty' (2009); Potts (1990) vol.1
